title: The foolishness of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18–31)
hook: God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise
tomorrow: how did the great Paul first walk into Corinth?

segments.voice: A week from a king's hall to Corinth: a good wish with no pressure, good cheer in a storm, bread on the deck, a fire in the rain, an open door, and yesterday, is Christ divided?
screen: `IS CHRIST DIVIDED?` → `A WEEK FROM A KING'S HALL TO CORINTH.`

segments.voice: Some comedians make the joke about their weak spot before anyone else can. Paul does it with his whole message: "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." Why admit it? Because he's writing to a church arguing over whose teacher is wisest, and he won't pretend the cross sounds clever.
screen: `SAY THE WEAK SPOT FIRST.` → `FOOLISHNESS, OR THE POWER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Then he turns the word around: "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Even God's foolish side, he says, outthinks us. And he points at the readers: "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called". Look around the room. And that's on purpose: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise". So nobody gets to boast about a teacher or their own cleverness. Paul closes with a line he introduces as already written: "He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord." Now look back over the week, because it fits. A king said almost. A prisoner gave the pep talk on a sinking ship. People the King James calls barbarous were the kind ones. A chained man ended the book with an open door. Again and again, the one who looks weakest carries the story.
screen: `PAUL ADMITS IT SOUNDS FOOLISH.` · `GOD'S FOOLISHNESS, WISER.` · `NOT MANY WISE, NOT MANY MIGHTY.` · `THE WEEK'S WEAK ONES CARRY IT.` · then, large: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Find one plain thing near you that nobody would pay much for: a worn mug, an old pencil, a stone from somewhere. Look at it for the whole sit, and let it be worth something without defending it.
The foolishness of the cross. Paul's phrase for a message that sounds foolish to some, and that he calls the power of God.
screen: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the week's end: the foolishness of God, wiser than men, and the weak ones who carry the story. Week done.

howItsDone: Some Christians read 1 Corinthians 1 in seasons that focus on the cross, such as Holy Week, and some churches keep a cross at the front as a plain reminder of it.

match.prompt: the week's lines — tap the pairs.

myth: Paul says his message sounds wise to everyone
to some it's foolishness; to Paul it's the power of God.
Paul says not many of the Corinthians were mighty or noble
not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
in Acts 27, the ship's captain gave the pep talk
a prisoner did: be of good cheer, twice.

fork.setup: a friend says only clever, impressive people ever change anything. which of this week's scenes would Paul point to?
options: a prisoner calming a ship that had lost all hope.
a king who almost decided, in great pomp.
a governor shouting that much learning makes you mad.
fork.reveal: the prisoner, not the captain, said be of good cheer. Paul's point: God chose the weak things of the world to confound the mighty.

original.note: Greek: foolishness. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 1:18 for how the cross sounds to some.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross as a symbol everyone respects.
what it means: Paul admits it sounded foolish to some, and calls that foolishness wiser than men.

chat.says: a guy here called our final hymn 'cringe, nobody believes this stuff.' half the room laughed. i didn't.
options: Paul admitted the cross sounds foolish to some. You can sing it anyway, no speech needed.
Prove him wrong: give him every reason the hymn makes sense until he admits it.
Laugh along so it's not weird, and save the real singing for church back home.
chat.meaning: Paul didn't pretend the cross sounds clever. He let it sound foolish to some and called it the power of God.

brethren.meaning: old English for brothers; here, the church's members

barbarous.meaning: the King James word for the islanders of Malta
